2.text: both circumstances. The Chukchee, notwithstanding their quick temper, still

3.text: have in their character a streak of soberness. “Large profits are always

4.text: preferable to blood,” they say. I have described above in some detail the

5.text: Anui-fair murder, where the Russians paid weregild for the killed man. The

6.text: Chukchee, even in the hottest of the quarrel, did not express a direct craving

7.text: for the blood of the murderer. I should, however, mention that the scuffle

8.text: was so sudden and disorderly, that the natives did not notice who of the Rus-

9.text: sians dealt the mortal blow to the victim. The Russians knew, but of course

10.text: kept it a secret. The next year this man avoided going to the Anui fair.

11.text: Not knowing the name of the murderer, the Chaun people were disposed to

12.text: wreak their vengeance on the “chief,” Eiˊheli, as I have already mentioned.

13.text: The next year Eiˊheli also refused to go to the Anui fair; but the visit could

14.text: not be avoided because of his official duties. He, however, left all his rein-

15.text: deer far away, and was conveyed to the fair by the Russians on a dog-team.

16.text: He lived within the Russian fort, and avoided appearing in the trading-camps.

17.text: Some days after his coming, the brother of the killed man met him at the

18.text: house of the Russian chief officer, and promised to pay him a personal visit.

19.text: A few hours later Eiˊheli asked to be taken away from the fair, and carried

20.text: to Nishne-Kolymsk. “Otherwise they will kill me,” he persisted. “This time

21.text: I shall not escape.” So this case also might have ended in blood-revenge.

22.text: I mentioned another case where a Maritime Chukchee whose cousin had

23.text: been murdered in a reindeer-camp on the Anui River, took as weregild a young

24.text: boy of the family of the murderer, and also a large part of his herd. The

25.text: next year he came again and took another part of the herd of reindeer. He

26.text: gave as his reason for doing so that weregild must be taken three consecutive

27.text: years. Otherwise the spirit of the victim would not be appeased. His demands

28.text: were considered exorbitant. When he was driving the reindeer back to his

29.text: country, one of the kinsmen of the one killed crossed his path, and requested

30.text: that half of the animals be given back. The Reindeer man had other people

31.text: with him, and they immediately proceeded to divide the herd. “After that

32.text: close asking,” said the last comer, “we shall have enough of this. The next

33.text: year we shall fight you.” The brother of the man killed by the Russians

34.text: also mentioned three years of payment of weregild, but the third year he

35.text: got nothing. The whole value given to his step-father and to himself reached

36.text: about three hundred rubles. It consisted of tea, sugar, tobacco, kettles, colored

37.text: calico, etc. He asked also for some brandy; but this time the authorities

38.text: had brought none, and refused to grant the request. Thus, in these two cases

39.text: the weregild paid by the murderer was heavy enough.

40.text: In a third case of which I know, the weregild was much smaller. The

41.text: affair took place also at the Anui fair, in the year 1894. A man came there
